candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Faith is not evidence-based confidence but an excuse for belief when no good reason can be supplied.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly contrasts confidence grounded in evidence with faith lacking adequate reasons.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This distinction supplies the skeptical epistemic standard used throughout the exchange to challenge the claimed basis for Christian belief.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ray Comfort's characterization of confidence or trust as equivalent to religious faith.

candidates.contextSummary: The speakers compare evidence for a marriage with evidence for a divine relationship, leading to a dispute over whether confidence and faith are equivalent.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: A relationship with a spouse is demonstrable through independent evidence, whereas Ray's claimed relationship with God is not comparably demonstrable.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly explains the purpose of his marriage hypothetical and identifies the evidential disparity it is meant to expose.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The comparison directly challenges Ray's analogy between ordinary interpersonal relationships and an asserted relationship with an unseen deity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ray Comfort's attempt to place belief in his relationship with God on the same footing as belief in his marriage.

candidates.contextSummary: After testing marriage certificates and spousal testimony as possible verification, Matt states that the same forms of corroboration are unavailable for God.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Scriptural inspiration attributed to God may instead originate in the believer's own mind, with no reliable external method for distinguishing competing claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt develops an outsider test involving different people who each attribute a scriptural message to God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move challenges the explanatory reliability and public verifiability of personal revelation, a principal basis offered for Ray's divine relationship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ray Comfort's claim that God communicates with him daily through the words of scripture.

candidates.contextSummary: Ray says God speaks through scripture rather than an audible voice; Matt asks how an outsider could distinguish genuine revelation from private interpretation.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Taking God's existence, moral authority, and scripture on faith is not a sound method for reaching truth when those claims cannot be demonstrated.
candidates.attributionBasis: The sustained turn identifies several undemonstrated religious claims and explicitly criticizes faith as an epistemic methodology.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is a consolidated challenge to the explanatory foundation of the gospel account, arguing that its essential premises lack a truth-tracking basis.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ray Comfort's instruction to repent, trust Christ, and approach scripture through faith and humility.

candidates.contextSummary: Following Ray's claim that scripture becomes intelligible after trusting Christ, Matt rejects assumptions about his inner state and attacks faith-based justification generally.

candidates.speaker: Ray Comfort
candidates.proposition: Natural suffering is evidence of the biblical account because disease, disaster, pain, and death are consequences of living in a fallen creation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Ray directly answers the problem-of-evil question by connecting broad human suffering to the scriptural doctrine of a fallen creation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move offers the evangelical account's principal explanation for apparently unjust suffering and presents that suffering as corroboration rather than disconfirmation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The questioner's contention that childhood cancer and God's foreknowledge of Satan make God responsible and unjust.

candidates.contextSummary: A question invokes childhood cancer, Satan, divine foreknowledge, and responsibility; Ray broadens the issue to suffering generally and invokes the Fall.

candidates.speaker: Ray Comfort
candidates.proposition: Persistent religious disagreement results from humanity inventing gods in its own image, while the first commandment identifies a single true creator.
candidates.attributionBasis: Ray invokes the first commandment and develops idolatry as his explanation for the proliferation of rival conceptions of God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument addresses religious pluralism by preserving the exclusivity of the Christian God and explaining alternatives as human moral constructions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The questioner's challenge that prolonged debate has produced no agreement about which god is real or whether any gods exist.

candidates.contextSummary: Asked why centuries of debate have not resolved God's identity or existence, Ray contrasts one creator with human-made deities lacking binding moral demands.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: A creator able to make a different universe bears responsibility for foreseeable atrocities that occur in the universe it deliberately chose to create.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly connects divine creative alternatives with responsibility for Hitler and other preventable events.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly contests the moral coherence of absolving an omniscient creator while assigning responsibility only to created human agents.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ray Comfort's claim that perpetrators alone answer for atrocities and that God bears no responsibility for their actions.

candidates.contextSummary: Ray denies that God is responsible for Jeffrey Dahmer or Hitler and emphasizes judgment; Matt appeals to God's acknowledged ability to create differently.

candidates.speaker: Ray Comfort
candidates.proposition: God cares for fallen humanity by offering salvation through Christ's death to anyone who believes, regardless of ethnicity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Ray states the salvific function of Christ's death and describes the offer as open to whoever believes or trusts.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move succinctly presents the evangelical atonement and salvation claim at the center of the debate's contested gospel account.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Matt Dillahunty's questioning of whether God cares about people whom Ray says are not God's children.

candidates.contextSummary: After Ray distinguishes God's children from rebellious humanity, Matt presses whether God nevertheless cares for them, prompting Ray's gospel summary.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Because God already knows who will be saved, God could have created those people with him from the outset instead of creating the present world.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt draws a direct implication from divine foreknowledge to an available alternative act of creation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument challenges the explanatory necessity of earthly testing, suffering, and perdition within a salvation plan governed by complete foreknowledge.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ray Comfort's claim that God lovingly offers everlasting life through Christ to whoever believes.

candidates.contextSummary: Immediately after Ray describes an open offer of salvation, Matt argues that foreknowledge makes the existing route to heaven unnecessary.

candidates.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
candidates.proposition: Substitutionary payment may cancel a debt or repair damage, but it does not reform the wrongdoer's defective character or stop continued wrongdoing.
candidates.attributionBasis: Matt distinguishes removal of an obligation from correction of character and illustrates the distinction through unpaid bills and broken windows.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy directly attacks substitutionary atonement by arguing that transferred payment leaves the underlying moral agent and behavioral problem unchanged.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The debt-payment analogy offered in the audience question as a model for understanding another party's payment on behalf of a wrongdoer.

candidates.contextSummary: An audience question asks whether third-party debt payment changes an unreliable debtor; Matt explains why compensation does not itself transform the offender.
